decision: Elastic window: the discontinuous form (e = 1 below v_el, the paper's e(v) unchanged at and above it), applied to every collision type (pair, side wall, plate), with v_el a module constant in granular/edmd.py (0.01 on method/elastic-window, 0.03 on method/elastic-window-v003).
alternatives: Continuous variant 1 - B (v - v_el)^0.75 above the window
Window on plate collisions only
v_el as a Simulation argument
rationale: The discontinuous form is what the Nov 5 instruction specifies, and it leaves the paper's law exactly unchanged above v_el. Applying it to all collision types is what option 3 in notes/contact-options.md describes and covers lasting pair contacts, which take part in the stall (a sphere with a neighbour above it). A module constant lets the referee's long_contact.py run the branch unchanged, and the commit hash it records then identifies v_el exactly.

decision: Position nudge: after every plate event (including events where the sphere was already separating), raise the sphere to two floating-point steps above the plate surface (nextafter twice) when it is lower; never lower it. The potential energy added goes to the eighth accounting slot, en[EN_NUDGE].
alternatives: Set the height unconditionally, as astra does, which can also lower a sphere
One floating-point step
Nudge only after collisions that actually reversed the sphere
rationale: Raising only means the nudge can only add energy, so its whole effect shows up as a positive, exactly recorded term instead of partly cancelling. Two steps match the instruction ('one or two floating-point steps') and guarantee a strictly positive gap even after rounding of the plate position. A sphere leaving any plate event should have a positive gap, so skipped events are nudged too.

decision: Survival grid read as: Gamma 3.5 depth 15 at both frequencies; Gamma 5 at f* 0.3 for depths 5, 10, 15 and at f* 0.5 for depths 10 and 15 (every Gamma 5 point except depth 5, f* 0.5, which the unmodified engine runs); plus the 3D case. 2D at L = 100 with seed 1, the same as the unmodified engine's survival pilot, so outcomes compare condition by condition.
alternatives: Only f* 0.5 at Gamma 5 (the other reading of the instruction)
Several seeds per condition
rationale: These are exactly the conditions where the unmodified engine stalls in the survival pilot table, which is what the instruction asks for ('conditions where the unmodified engine stalls'). Seed 1 matches the pilot so the comparison is like for like; more seeds are for when a method looks promising.

decision: Method branches are tested with main's virtual environment and PYTHONPATH set to the worktree (frozen tests) or long_contact.py's --engine (survival, bulk), rather than a separate uv environment per worktree.
alternatives: uv sync inside each worktree
rationale: pyproject.toml points roborobo at ../research-programs, a relative path that doesn't resolve from sequel-data/worktrees/, so uv sync fails there. long_contact.py already checks that granular is imported from the engine path, and the frozen-test runs printed the imported path, so the engine under test is the branch's.

decision: Elastic-window survival runs (E0002, E0005) are capped at 1 CPU-hour each, not the 8 CPU-hours used for the nudge.
alternatives: 8 CPU-hours per run, as for the nudge
Up to the 40 CPU-hour per-run budget
rationale: In the pilot (E0001) both window runs entered a slow stretch in cycle 2 with hundreds of millions of plate collisions slower than 1e-10; one ended in a physical failure after 10 CPU-minutes and the other was still inside the same slow stretch at its 15-minute cap. Survival is measured as cycles completed before the stall, which a 1-hour cap records; a longer cap would spend up to 64 more CPU-hours mostly on the same open slow stretch. If a run is still progressing at its cap it can be resumed with --resume.

decision: Plate-stick sticks in the vertical only: the capture collision sets vz to the plate velocity and leaves horizontal velocity and spin unchanged, and a stuck sphere keeps its horizontal velocity and spin until freed.
alternatives: Apply the Walton friction impulse of an e = 0 collision at capture
Stick fully (horizontal velocity to zero) while stuck
rationale: Chris's stated default in the instruction of 2026-11-07. It changes the paper's collision model as little as possible: only the normal restitution of very slow plate collisions (below v_stick) becomes zero.

decision: No transitive sticking: a sphere resting on a stuck sphere stays free and keeps colliding with it under the paper's law.
alternatives: Stick stacks transitively (as the sonnet-5-max trial did)
rationale: Chris's stated default (instruction of 2026-11-07); transitive sticking is a model change. Expected cost: the rattle can move from the plate to the pair above it.

decision: v_stick = 1e-4 sqrt(gD) on method/plate-stick, with a pilot at 1e-3 on method/plate-stick-v1e-3 (identical code apart from the constant).
alternatives: Pick the value from the pilot alone
A runtime option instead of a branch per value
rationale: Chris's default and pilot value. A branch per value (as for the elastic window's v_el) keeps the value in the engine provenance long_contact.py records, with no hidden switch.

decision: A collision that changes a stuck sphere's velocity (with another sphere or a side wall) frees it; if it is then moving into the plate, the plate collision (with the capture rule) is applied at the same instant, before anything else is predicted.
alternatives: Treat a stuck sphere as an infinite mass moving with the plate (Gonzalez et al.'s frozen-particle rule)
Ignore collisions that would push a stuck sphere into the plate
rationale: Keeps every collision a binary collision with the paper's law; an infinite-mass rule would change the collision model for the upper sphere. Sequential resolution at one instant is the usual hard-sphere treatment of a three-body contact.

decision: After release (at a_p = -g, with the plate's velocity), the plate-contact search skips the interval in which the gap, growing as jerk t^3/6, is below 1e-12 D.
alternatives: Nudge the sphere upward at release
Keep it stuck slightly past release
rationale: At the release point gap, gap rate and gap curvature are all exactly zero, so round-off can produce spurious zero-time plate roots after release (when a_p < -g, capture cannot absorb them). Skipping an interval where contact is analytically impossible changes no physics and adds no energy; a nudge would add energy, and staying stuck would pull the sphere down.

decision: Softer initial conditions for the case-b baseline are made with the engine's own Simulation constructor arguments fill_fraction and v_init (identical on main and every method branch), written as a cycle-0 checkpoint (sequel-data/runs/tools/soft_start.py) that referee/long_contact.py then runs with --resume. Three variants are piloted against the default (fill 0.30, v_init 0.1): hot (fill 0.30, v_init 1.0), hot dilute (fill 0.10, v_init 1.0), cold dilute (fill 0.10, v_init 0.1). Whichever gets the unmodified engine through, if any, is used for every engine at case b.
alternatives: Ask Chris to add initial-condition options to long_contact.py (the referee is his)
Ramp Gamma up from zero over the first cycles (an engine change, so not identical across engines)
Start from a settled state produced by the nudge (method-dependent)
rationale: The default start is a loose slab resting on the plate at phase 0, so the first landing is a coherent slab; a hot or dilute start spreads the first landings in time. Using constructor arguments that already exist changes no engine code, so the initial state is the same for every engine at a given seed; the referee's loop, audit and output are used unchanged (it reads the cycle-0 checkpoint exactly as it reads its own). An option in long_contact.py would be cleaner and is proposed to Chris.

decision: Within E0019, the cold-dilute start (fill 0.10, v_init 0.1) is rerun at seeds 1 and 2 with --cycles 1020, --checkpoint-every 2 and an 8 CPU-hour cap, because both pilot runs passed cycle one cleanly and hit the 1 CPU-hour pilot cap inside cycle two (the dilute layer's first landing) without a slow episode or failure; the pilot's only checkpoint was at cycle 0, so it could not be resumed.
alternatives: Stop at the pilot: no variant got both seeds through 3 cycles
Resume the pilot runs (impossible: checkpoint at cycle 0 only)
rationale: The pilot cap was a cost choice, not a result; the cold-dilute runs are the only ones that neither failed nor stalled. Every other variant failed within two cycles (standard seeds 4 and 1, 2 earlier; hot seed 2; hot-dilute seeds 1 and 2), and hot seed 1 was inside a slow episode at its cap.

decision: In E0024, where the unmodified engine fails its L = 400 baseline (Gamma 5 f* 0.5 depth 5: overlap at cycle 51, seed 1; Gamma 3.5 f* 0.3 depth 10: overlap in cycle 1 at seed 1, slow first landing at seed 2), the baseline is the 1998 C code at L = 400 (referee/c_baseline.py, 1020 cycles, seeds 16532 1 2 in order), measured with bulk.py baseline and then its trajectory deleted (2.4 and 4.7 GB), keeping the baseline JSON with its checksum. One C run at a time, so disk stays under the program budget.
alternatives: More seeds of the unmodified engine (its failure at L 400 comes from lasting contacts, which a bigger box only makes more likely)
Judge these two conditions at L 100 instead
rationale: The referee's rule (BRIEF.md, referee/README.md): where this engine stalls, the C code is the baseline. L = 400 follows the instruction for all 2D bulk checks.

decision: Recorded after the fact (made Nov 7 in commit 3900896 on method/plate-stick, without a record): in stuck_pair_root, a stuck-free pair in contact (gap below 1e-12 D) whose approach speed is below STUCK_VN_MIN = 1e-12 is not a collision; if the pair is pressed (f'' < 0) the search steps forward to where the approach speed is 10 x STUCK_VN_MIN, otherwise it steps on as if separating.
alternatives: Treat a pressed stuck-free pair as a collision with the stuck sphere as an infinite mass moving with the plate (the paper's law, as a plate collision)
Capture the free sphere onto the stuck one (transitive sticking; ruled out by Chris's default)
Accept the zero-speed contact as a collision (the pilot's freeze, E0021)
rationale: Without it the pilot froze: zero-speed contacts gave zero-time collisions. E0026 shows its cost: the pair collides every 2.5e-12 time units without separating, a stall, and rounding over millions of such steps builds the overlap that ends every plate-stick run. Neither alternative is available without a change Chris reserves (the first changes the collision model for the upper sphere, D0009; the second is transitive sticking). Kept on the branch as a record of what plate-stick does; not proposed for further use.

decision: Design for option 4 (persistent contact) in a vibrated layer, for Chris to approve or amend before any code: evidence/D0015-option4-design.md. Spheres at rest relative to the plate (stuck on it, or frozen on stuck or frozen supporters) ride it rigidly; freezing at a slow, downward, decelerating collision with a stuck or frozen sphere (V_sleep 1e-4 sqrt(gD)); slow hits on frozen spheres use the plate collision (infinite mass, the paper's law); waking at release (a_p = -g, all together), on supporter loss (cascade), or by a hit above V_wakeup (1e-2 sqrt(gD)); dissipative only, no stored energy returned.
alternatives: Transitive sticking on plate-stick (vertical-only, no freezing of sliding)
González's alpha_frozen restitution for hits on frozen spheres
A geometric stability test (centre above the hull of contacts) instead of one supporter
rationale: E0026 shows plate-stick's remaining lasting contact is a free sphere pressed on a plate-riding sphere, which only a resting state for that sphere removes. The five choices listed at the end of the note change the model or add constants and are Chris's to make.

decision: Redesign of option 4 (persistent contact), per the 2026-11-09 instruction, for Chris to approve or amend before any code: evidence/D0016-option4-redesign.md. One resting state (at rest in the plate frame), the plate a supporter that never wakes, modelled on Gonzalez's rotating drum (plate frame = fixed floor with time-varying effective gravity g + a_p, as the drum frame has fixed walls with rotating gravity). Sleep below V_sleep relative to the plate; wake when g_eff reaches zero (all at once), on supporter loss (cascade), or by a hit above V_wakeup; slow hits on resting spheres use the plate law. Every cutoff is a setting with a sweep range; V_sleep = 0 must reproduce main bit for bit. Six code versions, each with its tests. Over-aggressive resting is checked by packing fraction against height with and without resting, and by a deposition test against Gonzalez's phi = 0.640 - 0.11 V_t.
alternatives: D0015's separate stuck and frozen states
Gonzalez's alpha_frozen = 0.4 for hits on resting spheres
Geometric (hull) stability as the default
Gonzalez's stored-energy return as the default
rationale: The instruction asked for one resting state with the plate as a supporter, modelled on the drum; the drum's frozen wall and rotating gravity map directly onto the plate and g_eff. Chatter above V_sleep is kept and resolved with the paper's law; only the Zeno tail below V_sleep is replaced by rest, which makes the remaining chatter finite (about 4.4 V_sleep^-0.75 bounces per contact for a single sphere).

decision: Queue policy from Nov 10: one queue script (sequel-data/runs/tools/qx3.sh) caps live simulations across all experiments together (8, leaving two of the ten budgeted cores for analysis) and launches nothing while free disk is below 40.5 GB. The per-experiment queue for E0031 (qx.sh, 3 at a time) was stopped at 23:10 with its three running jobs left alive, and its 15 unlaunched lines plus E0034's five were put in one spec (nudge continuations first, then E0034, then the two slow unmodified-engine runs). Simulations already running when the disk fell below the floor are not killed.
alternatives: Launch the small runs anyway (each writes a few MB; the shortfall is swap from other work, not program data)
Kill the three running simulations as well
Keep per-experiment caps

decision: Case-b main baseline (E0037): burn-in fixed at 300 cycles and 7 baseline blocks of 100 per seed from 1000-cycle runs, judged with bulk.py's threshold for 7 blocks. alternatives: Burn-in 20 cycles (referee default), 9 blocks
Run to 1320 cycles for a full 10-block baseline after 300 cycles of burn-in
Pool blocks across seeds
rationale: The instruction fixes 1000 cycles and asks for the burn-in to be fixed in the registration. decision: Details of persistent contact v1 to v3 not fixed by D0016: (1) the sleep test compares both the sphere's full translational speed relative to the plate and its spin surface speed r|w| with v_sleep, because resting sets velocity and spin to the plate's; (2) a hit wakes a resting sphere when the normal approach speed (relative to the resting sphere, which moves with the plate) exceeds v_wakeup, and a slow hit (v_sleep up to v_wakeup) is a plate-law collision with the impulse along the line of centres (Nov 11 instruction); (3) 'slower than at the previous collision' uses the speed relative to the plate measured at the sphere's previous collision of any kind; (4) downward_only on a sphere supporter means the supporter's centre is below the hitter's and the hitter moves down relative to the plate; (5) rest height is kept exactly (no snap to the surface), so resting moves no sphere; (6) method state lives in separate arrays X and SUP, not in S, so S keeps eight columns; (7) the intrinsic sweep adds v_wakeup = v_sleep (no middle band), per the Nov 11 instruction.
alternatives: Sleep on vertical (normal) relative speed only, as plate-stick did
Wake on full relative speed
Previous-collision speed from plate collisions only
Snap resting spheres to the surface (plate-stick did, which books an unaccounted m g dz)
rationale: Each choice keeps D0016's resting state (at rest in the plate frame, no spin) consistent: a sphere is only stopped when everything it loses is below the threshold, so resting removes at most about m v_sleep^2 per sphere. The normal speed is what sets the impulse of a hit. Not snapping keeps every energy change booked, so the audit can be exact.

decision: Question for Chris, from a v3 unit test: a sphere rolling on the plate never satisfies the approved rest rule (full speed below v_sleep), so its vertical bounces still accumulate without end while g_eff > 0 (a sphere bounced off a resting one at 2e-3, rolled off at about 0.08, and stalled on a Gamma 0.5 plate). The model has no rolling resistance, so nothing stops the rolling. Default: keep the approved rule, and find out from the v3 pilots (E0039) whether any stall is a sphere rolling on the plate or on resting spheres before changing anything.
alternatives: On the plate only, rest on the normal (vertical) relative speed and keep the horizontal velocity and spin while resting, so a resting sphere can roll or slide along the plate (plate-stick's stuck state; changes D0016's resting state)

Treat a sphere whose normal speed is below v_sleep but whose tangential speed is above it as rolling contact: integrate it on the plate surface with no bounces until it reaches another sphere or g_eff = 0 (new state, more code)
Add rolling resistance (a model change, out of scope without asking)
rationale: The approved rule removes all of a resting sphere's energy, which is small only when the sphere is slow in every direction; stopping a rolling sphere at 0.08 would remove far more than m v_sleep^2. Whether the case matters in a layer is an empirical question the pilots answer.

decision: Merge fix/energy-accumulators (901a971) into main and carry it to every method branch: run_events sums the energy and impulse terms of each call in a local array from zero and adds them to the run totals once, instead of adding every event's change to run-long totals. Trajectories are bit-identical. Then re-judge audit failures (both engines) from runs made with it.
alternatives: Kahan-compensated summation into the run totals
Leave the engine and have the referee reset the totals each cycle (referee is Chris's)
Leave as is and treat chatter-cycle residuals as known noise
rationale: E0031 replay: in one collision-heavy window the residual is 2.1e-6 with the totals at 1.6e6 and 1.4e-11 with the totals started at zero, same trajectory. So audit failures in long chatter-heavy runs, of either sign and for any engine, are at least partly round-off in the bookkeeping, not energy put in or lost by a contact method. The energy audit is part of the 'contact method works' evidence, so this should be fixed before it is used to accept or reject a method. Merging into main is Chris's call (DIRECTION.md).

decision: Normal rest rule as built on method/persistent-contact-normal (9923d8a, 8b78fec), details not fixed by the Nov 12 instruction: (1) a new setting rest_rule = normal; the default stays full (D0016) so the approved design and its tests are untouched; (2) on the plate only the vertical velocity relative to the plate is stopped; horizontal velocity and spin are kept, and the energy removed is the vertical kinetic energy in the plate frame; (3) nothing rests on a sphere under the normal rule (that part is proposed in D0024, not built); (4) 'slower than at the previous collision' compares vertical speeds relative to the plate, and a sphere woken by a hit has no previous speed; (5) a resting sphere that slides into a side wall wakes, and two resting spheres that slide into each other both wake and collide by the paper's law; (6) hits on a resting sphere: first built as 'every hit wakes it' (normal_hit = wake), then, after E0042 showed that this collapses a pressed pair, a second variant normal_hit = held: a hit slower than v_wakeup from above is one collision in which the plate holds the resting sphere vertically and it recoils horizontally, with the paper's restitution on the normal relative speed. Held is frictionless only.
alternatives: Keep D0016's slow-hit rule (infinite mass along the line of centres) for a sliding resting sphere
Wake on every hit only
Rest on spheres with the v3 state (stops the tangential motion)
rationale: D0016's slow-hit rule treats the resting sphere as immovable. Once it slides, that holds it against horizontal impulses: horizontal momentum is not conserved and the pressing force does work on a moving obstacle, which the frictionless plate cannot supply. Waking uses only the paper's laws but its recapture has zero restitution, a fixed fractional loss per hit, and E0042 showed the collapse that follows (1.04e8 sleep/wake pairs and an overlap at v_sleep 1e-3). The held hit conserves horizontal momentum, loses only what the paper's restitution loses, and books the plate's impulse and work. These are changes to how slow hits are treated, which D0016 put in Chris's hands; they are on a branch and need his decision before they go further.

decision: How tonight's runs set parameters the referee does not expose. referee/long_contact.py builds Simulation with the engine's defaults, so: (1) frictionless and pilot settings are the defaults of pinned one-commit branches (method/mu0-unmodified 765c1f0, method/persistent-contact-normal-mu0 b40bfd4, method/persistent-contact-normal-held-mu0 cba8c0c), none for merging; (2) every run goes through tools/lc_counters.py, which calls the referee's main() unchanged and writes the engine's counters, friction coefficient and contact settings to counters.json when the run ends, so sleeps and wakes are known even when a run never checkpoints; (3) the v_sleep sweeps and the friction scan change one default per run through the wrapper's environment variables (SEQUEL_CONTACT_OVERRIDE, SEQUEL_MU), recorded in counters.json, rather than one branch per value.
alternatives: One branch per setting
A separate driver instead of the referee
Ask for a settings option in long_contact.py (Chris's file)
rationale: The Nov 11 pilots could not show whether the method acted because counters were only in checkpoints, and three runs used a different commit from the registered one. Pinned commits keep the referee's provenance record true; the wrapper records what the referee does not. An option in long_contact.py would be cleaner and is listed under referee findings.

decision: For Chris: how tangential motion is handled when a sphere rests on a sphere under the normal rule. Proposal (evidence/D0024-rest-on-sphere-proposal.md): tangent-plane rest with re-capture. The normal relative velocity is stopped; the upper sphere keeps its tangential velocity and moves in the plane tangent to the supporter; that takes it off the surface by a positive gap, and when the gap reaches a set size it is freed and captured again. With friction, add closed-form sliding friction on the plate and on the tangent plane, and rolling contact. Default if unanswered: build the frictionless tangent-plane rest on a branch and test it on the E0042 failure case.
alternatives: Rigid rest when the tangential speed is also below v_sleep (v3)
Exact motion on the supporter's sphere (no closed form)
Leave the upper sphere free and make slow hits lossless (held)
rationale: E0043: in the stalled pairs both contacts carry tangential motion (rolling at 0.03 to 0.65), so rigid rest never applies. E0042: any fixed fractional loss in the hit path collapses a pressed pair, so the upper sphere needs a state of its own rather than more collisions. The tangent-plane error is always a positive gap, never an overlap, and its size is set by v_sleep.

decision: Reading of the fallback instruction for the night of Nov 14 (no instruction from Chris). decision: Item 5 build (method/held-contact): (a) trigger: a plate hit, or a hit on an already held sphere, with normal closing speed below v_hold = 1e-2 sqrt(gD) is captured (no new trigger on a pair of free spheres, as the instruction's 'ball on plate, then ball on a held ball'); (b) holding by impulses along the contact normal every dt_hold = 1e-4 sqrt(D/g), solved jointly for a held cluster by projected Gauss-Seidel so that each contact stays closed over the next step in free flight, pushes only; (c) release when a contact's impulse is zero (its force would be a pull) or when it is hit faster than v_hold (then an ordinary collision with the paper's law); (d) tangential motion free: no friction impulse and no spin change in a held contact (the paper's sliding friction impulse goes to zero with the normal speed); (e) 'motion on the sphere' re-aligns a sphere-sphere normal every step, 'fixed angle' keeps the capture normal and lets go beyond a gap of 1e-4 D; (f) side walls held like the plate (found necessary: chatter against a wall under a held cluster); (g) a capture counts as a collision of its kind in the event counters; the energy change of hold steps beyond the plate's work is booked as plate dissipation and separately in EN_HOLD, and steps that gain energy are counted in their own counter (C_HGAIN), not in the collision-gain counter.
rationale: The instruction fixes the rule (normal velocity held at zero, tangential free, let go at a pull, two ways to move the upper sphere) and leaves the trigger, step and numerics open. Impulses at fixed steps keep the event-driven core unchanged between steps and bound the event rate of a contact by 1/dt_hold instead of letting it collapse in time. v_hold 1e-2 is far above the speeds of a collapsing contact (1e-10) and far below ordinary impacts; dt_hold 1e-4 keeps the step's own closing speed (up to (g + Gamma g) dt, 6e-4 at Gamma 5) well below v_hold. Point (g) keeps the referee's audit meaningful: the hold steps' energy change is a discretisation of a force that does no work in the contact frame, so it is reported, with sign, rather than counted as collision gains.
alternatives: count recent collisions of the same pair as the trigger (Chris: contact duration is collisions)

count hold-step gains in the referee's collision-gain counter (every Gamma 5 cycle would then fail the audit on a discretisation term of order 1e-8)

decision: Held contacts v2 (9860a26), changed before the survival runs went further: a hit faster than v_hold on a held sphere frees it (all its held contacts become ordinary collisions) instead of re-solving its cluster; the solver starts from the previous step's impulses, over-relaxes (1.5) after an exact first sweep and stops at a relative change of 1e-8; dt_hold is 5e-4 instead of 1e-4.

decision: Held contacts v3 (df3f4dc): a collision between two free spheres closing slower than 1e-10 (the engine's existing 'tiny collision' speed) is captured as a held pair, like a slow hit on a held sphere.

decision: Gap-limited friction in held contacts: after computing each plate or wall friction impulse, scan all particles and scale the impulse to prevent the held sphere from drifting into overlap with any touching non-cluster neighbour over one dt_hold. Post-step re-prediction tolerance narrowed from 1e-3 to 1e-6. Friction remains off by default until the remaining overlaps are resolved.
rationale: The root cause of friction overlap is friction drift: each hold step changes the held sphere's horizontal velocity, causing drift of about 2.3e-7 per dt_hold into touching neighbours, exceeding the 2e-8 overlap tolerance after one step. The gap limiter prevents this for isolated pairs but is partial: it delays failures from cycle 1 to cycle 10-11.

decision: Stopping rule for the settle-then-step ramp (E0090): run each step in blocks of 50 cycles. After 200 cycles, compare two 100-cycle windows (each split into two 50-cycle blocks). For each quantity (pattern amplitude A and layer height), the block standard error of the reference window (previous 100 cycles) is |block1 - block2| / 2. The step is settled when |mean_last100 - mean_prev100| < 2 SE for both quantities. Per-block amplitude is the noise-corrected band amplitude from loop_analysis.py (BAND_LO = 3, same correction), computed from the 1600 frames of the block. Per-block thickness is the mean of the 1600 frame values of the referee's thickness quantity. Minimum 200, maximum 3000 cycles per step.
alternatives: Per-cycle values for the SE (100 values per window; tighter but ignores autocorrelation)
Pooling all blocks in the step for the SE (better estimate, but the reference is the whole run rather than the recent window)
Blocks of 25 (more blocks per window, but less averaging per block)
rationale: Blocks of 50 and windows of 100 are what the instruction specifies. The block SE with 1 degree of freedom is noisy but naturally accounts for the within-block correlation (decorrelation time is 5 to 13 cycles per Nov 8 findings). With 2 blocks per window, 2 SE equals |block1 - block2|: the shift between windows must be smaller than the variation within the reference window. This is a loose but honest test.

decision: Analytical-motion contact method: rigid-body cluster coupling for v1. A riding sphere's position is locked to a fixed 3D offset from its supporter (plate or sphere), so the trajectory is sinusoidal plus a constant. All velocity components matched to the supporter at capture (fully inelastic). Release at the closed-form phase where plate acceleration equals minus g.
alternatives: Sliding coupling: constrain only the normal direction, let tangential velocity evolve freely. More physical but the tangential motion under sinusoidal forcing is not analytically solvable.
Normal-only coupling with periodic sub-steps for the tangential part (a hybrid of analytical and clusterlifter approaches).
rationale: Rigid coupling makes every sphere's trajectory fully analytical (closed-form) with no numerical time-stepping. It is the simplest design that handles both plate and sphere-on-sphere contacts. The held-contact's fixed-angle variant churned because of the dt_hold impulse mechanism, not because of the fixed angle itself; without periodic impulses the same problem should not arise. If rigid coupling causes artifacts, v2 or v3 can add sliding.

decision: Ride v2 sphere-on-sphere capture: a free sphere is captured onto a riding sphere when the contact normal points up from the riding sphere to the free one (any positive vertical component), the normal closing speed is below v_capture (1e-4), and the plate's acceleration is above minus g. Its vertical velocity becomes the plate's; the whole cluster's horizontal velocity becomes the mass-weighted mean of the cluster's and the newcomer's, so horizontal momentum is conserved. A hit or side-wall collision on a riding sphere releases it and every sphere riding on it (directly or through others), not the whole cluster.
alternatives: Match all three velocity components of the newcomer to its supporter without changing the cluster (D0058's first reading): does not conserve horizontal momentum and can add energy when the supporter moves faster horizontally.
Require a near-vertical normal (for example above 45 degrees) before capturing: fewer spheres locked by side contacts, but adds a tuned angle.
Release the whole cluster on any hit: simpler, but frees plate riders that weren't touched into an exactly-zero gap with the plate, where the plate root search is fragile.
rationale: Momentum-conserving merge makes capture a perfectly inelastic collision in the frame moving with the plate, so it can only remove energy, which the referee's audit can check. The plate supplies the vertical impulse through the supporter chain, booked as plate impulse and work. Releasing only the dependents keeps untouched riders on their analytic trajectories.

decision: Chris's answers of Nov 24 to the five choices in lines/L0009/design.md, as now built into method/rest: (1) a sphere may ride on a rolling sphere, so moving stacks are allowed (design section 6); (2) the wake speed is higher than the rest speed, a parameter with default 0.05 sqrt(gD); (3) the rest speed is a parameter with default 0.01 sqrt(gD); (4) the paper's store-and-return of energy removed at freezing is dropped; (5) the balance test lets friction (0.5 times each contact's push) help hold a sphere still.
alternatives: the D0069 defaults: only plate and still spheres carry riders; wake speed equal to rest speed
rationale: Chris answered each choice on the dashboard (lines/L0009/instruction.md, Nov 24 23:13-23:14). The number 0.05 for the wake speed is the agent's: Chris said 'make it higher' and that it is to be tuned later; 0.05 is five times the rest speed and inside the paper's range 0.01 to 0.5. Both speeds are RestParams fields, not constants.

decision: A hit on a still sphere with approach speed between the rest speed and the wake speed bounces the hitter off the still sphere as off an immovable body moving with the plate, using the base model's restitution law e(v) and Walton's tangential rule (the operator the engine already uses for walls, with the still sphere's surface moving at the plate velocity and no spin). The paper's restitution 0.4 on frozen spheres is not used.
alternatives: the paper's constant restitution 0.4 against frozen spheres
waking the still sphere on every hit faster than the rest speed (one threshold)
rationale: Chris chose a wake speed above the rest speed, so hits in between need a rule. Using the base model's own law keeps the collision model and its constants unchanged (DIRECTION.md puts changing them out of scope); 0.4 would be a new constant. The momentum goes to the plate, and the energy change is booked as plate work and plate dissipation like a plate hit.

decision: The balance test is a linear-programming feasibility check (phase one of the simplex method, Bland's rule) on contact forces. In 3D each contact's friction cone is replaced by the inscribed pyramid with 8 edges (RestParams.n_friction_dirs); in the planar (dim=2) case the cone is exact.
alternatives: an exact second-order cone test
a circumscribed pyramid (lets slightly more spheres rest)
rationale: An inscribed pyramid can only call a sphere unable to rest when a true cone could just hold it, never the reverse, so it errs toward riding (integrated, physical) rather than resting (frozen). The edge cases it changes are friction-limited seats within cos(pi/8), about 8 percent, of the friction limit. No scipy in the project, and contacts per sphere are few, so a small dense simplex suffices.

decision: Moving stacks (riders on riding spheres, allowed by D0073) are moved as one rigid-body system with lasting contacts: between events its equations of motion are a smooth ordinary differential equation whose contact forces come from a small linear solve at each evaluation (normal forces holding each lasting contact's approach acceleration at zero, friction either holding slip at zero or sliding at 0.5 times the push). It is integrated by an adaptive high-order integrator at round-off tolerance with dense output, and every change of a contact's state (a push reaching zero, slip stopping, rolling needing more than 0.5 times the push, a collision with a free sphere, the plate's release) is a located root of that dense output, handled as an event. Guard against a time-stepped code in disguise: no fixed time step, no impulses or position corrections at steps, no energy removed per step, the integrator's steps never change any contact's state, and the engine counts integrator steps and the share of sphere-time spent in integrated stacks so the cost is visible.
alternatives: first build without moving stacks (the D0069 default, overruled by Chris)
a time-stepped or iterative impulse solver for stacks (rejected by Chris: no time-stepped code in sheep's clothing)
rationale: A rider on a rolling sphere pushes on it, so the two cannot be moved separately; the forces between them are determined by the constraint that the contact neither opens nor penetrates. Solving those forces as part of a smooth ODE keeps each state change at its exact time, which is the event-driven principle; a stepped solver would detect changes late and need tolerances. The design is falsified as a speed-up if integrated stacks take most of the sphere-time in a dense layer; that share is measured, not assumed.

decision: The plate captures a sphere at a plate collision when the relative vertical speed is below the rest speed in size, whether the sphere is approaching or, by round-off, already separating, provided the plate is pushing (effective gravity g - A om^2 sin(om t) > 0). Approaching spheres get Walton's wall collision with normal restitution zero (friction impulse of the base model); a separating one only has its vertical velocity set to the plate's. All changes are booked as plate collision terms.
alternatives: capture approaching spheres only, leaving the round-off-separating ones to bounce (they return at once while the plate pushes, the stall's seed)
a separate tangential rule at capture
rationale: A sphere touching a plate that pushes upward cannot separate, so a tiny separating speed is round-off; capturing it is what the design means by rest. Keeping the base model's friction impulse leaves the collision model unchanged apart from the normal restitution of a capture, which the design already sets to zero.

decision: Until stacks are in the event loop, any collision with a riding sphere, and a riding sphere reaching a side wall, frees it and the ordinary collision happens, whatever the speed. The plate recaptures it if it is still slow.
alternatives: refuse to run until stacks exist
capture the hitter into a stack below the rest speed (the design; stage three, not built)
rationale: It lets the plate part be tested on its own. It is known to be wrong for a sphere resting on a riding sphere, and the first 2D layer showed exactly that (evidence/L0009-build-2026-11-25-2.json), so it is temporary.

decision: The compiled contact searches between a riding sphere and another sphere refuse an overlap deeper than 2e-8, the engine's existing limit for pairs (PAIR_PENETRATION_TOL), instead of the 1e-13 in squared distance used before; a pair counts as touching when its squared-distance gap is within 1e-13.
alternatives: keep the tighter refusal and look for where round-off exceeds it
rationale: After a collision followed by a capture in the same instant, a pair touches with an overlap of about 5e-14 in distance, which the old refusal treated as a failure. The engine's own limit is the established line between round-off and a missed event; no new tolerance is introduced.

decision: At capture the sphere's centre is put exactly on the plate (it is off by round-off after the collision search); the potential-energy change is booked as plate work and the largest such correction is kept (EN_MAX_SNAP) so it stays visible.
alternatives: let the ride start from the uncorrected height (the closed-form ride puts the centre on the plate anyway)
rationale: The closed-form ride defines the height as plate plus radius, so the correction happens either way; doing it at capture puts it in the books at the moment it happens and makes its size measurable. It was 0 in the one-sphere check.

decision: The stack integrator looks for an event function (a push, a friction margin, a slip) that goes below zero and recovers inside one accepted step by sampling the step's dense output (Dormand-Prince continuous extension) at 7 interior points, plus the minimum of a parabola through each three samples; the first sample at or below zero starts a bisection from the step start. It is a sampling test, not a bound: a dip narrower than about one eighth of a step and shallower than the parabola predicts can still be missed.
alternatives: a rigorous bound on each event function over the step (like first_root's conservative advancement), which needs bounds on the force solve's time derivatives that do not exist in closed form
cap the step so each event function changes by less than its value (costs many more steps when a push is near zero, which is exactly when stacks matter)
rationale: Steps at rtol 1e-12 are already short against the stack's motion, so a dip inside one step is rare; the sampling catches every smooth dip whose width is a sizeable fraction of a step and costs about 80% more force solves. On the existing physical stack cases it never fired and the results are identical bit for bit, so it changes nothing that was already right.

decision: Stacks will run with the compiled event loop this way: when a stack forms or changes, Python (granular/stack.py) integrates it ahead, up to its next internal contact change or a horizon, and stores the trajectory as dense-output segments in arrays the compiled loop can read. Free spheres' contact searches against stack spheres evaluate those segments (conservative advancement, as for plate riders). The compiled loop returns to Python (a new status) only at a stack's internal event, at its horizon, or when a free sphere hits a stack sphere. stack.py is not compiled until the share of time spent in stacks is measured.
alternatives: compile stack.py with numba now (a large rewrite before knowing whether stacks are rare)
return to Python at every stack step (makes free-sphere predictions against stack spheres impossible inside the compiled loop)
rationale: The free spheres' contact searches need the stack spheres' positions at arbitrary times inside the compiled loop; stored segments give that without moving the integrator into numba. Returning to Python only at stack events keeps the ordinary collisions in compiled code and makes the cost of stacks directly measurable (time in Python per cycle), which is what the open question to Chris needs.

decision: When a stack starts, any contact whose rolling would need more friction than mu times its push starts sliding (worst first, re-solving after each switch), and the stack integrator refuses to start with a violated condition. A sliding contact at zero slip (one that has just started to slide) takes its friction direction from the friction rolling would have needed, which is the direction the slip grows against.
alternatives: start every contact rolling and let the integrator find the switch (it cannot: a condition already violated at the start never crosses zero; the stall replay ran this way silently)
zero friction at exactly zero slip, as the earlier code did (an error of order mu N over the first stage of the first step, not round-off)
rationale: It is Coulomb's law applied at the stack's start, the same rule the integrator applies at a located 'slide' event. In the stall replay the top contact needed 1.10 times mu N, so this is a real case in the first stall, not a corner.

decision: At a stack's start, every contact labelled rolling whose tangential slip exceeds 1e-13 (SLIP0, the round-off floor already used for the friction direction) starts sliding with friction against its slip; the integrator refuses to start a rolling contact slipping by more than 1e-9. A driver (stack.evolve) runs a stack through its slide/roll changes until a contact opens. A sliding contact's return to rolling is located to about 1e-10 in time, not round-off: once the slip passes zero, sliding friction flips inside the bisection's trial steps, so the event function is not monotone there (measured 4.0e-11 late on a sphere sliding on a still plate).
alternatives: accept a rolling contact with slip below a physical tolerance (would add a tuned constant)
start every rider-to-plate contact sliding and let the integrator find rolling (equivalent for slipping contacts, but makes resting ones pass through a zero-length slide)
rationale: The checker's review of 2026-11-25-L0009-2 found the stall replay's plate contact labelled rolling with slip 0.0171, held constant for 0.40 time units with friction work booked on it (two of three stalls it looked at). Coulomb's law says such a contact slides until its slip is zero. In the replay both contacts slip at the start (0.0171 and 0.0421); the plate contact now slides for 0.0038 time units and then rolls.

decision: In the compiled event loop, a sphere touching a plate rider with a normal approach slower than v_rest no longer frees the rider (D0078, temporary); run_events returns a new status 2 with the event left at the head of the queue, and Simulation.build_stack makes the moving stack there. The residual approach is removed as a restitution-zero touch against the rider, which the plate holds: the upper sphere loses one half m vn squared in the rider's frame (dissipation), and the rest of its lab-frame energy change is the plate's work through the rider. Above v_rest the old rule (rider freed, ordinary collision) stays until the v_rest to v_wake band is built (D0074).
alternatives: remove the approach from the upper sphere and book the lab-frame energy change as dissipation (that change can be a gain: it was -0.0013, i.e. +0.0013 energy, in the stall layer, because the rider moves with the plate)
process the touch as an ordinary collision first and form the stack after (the chatter of the Nov 25 stall)
rationale: It is the design's hand-off point (design.md section 6, D0082) and replaces the rule that caused the stall. Booking in the rider's frame keeps the touch a pure loss plus plate work, as the plate capture (D0077) does.

decision: Per-cycle cost of an E0089 step stopped on the CPU cap is divided by covered cycles: completed cycles plus counters.json event_time over the drive period sqrt(depth)/f*. The old per-completed-cycle columns stay in evidence/E0089-step-table.json for traceability; findings quote the covered-cycle columns.
alternatives: Keep per-completed-cycle figures with a bound (fails at one completed cycle)
Use field-recorder frame counts (resolution 1/32 cycle)
rationale: The counters and CPU time cover the unfinished last cycle as well. With 21 to 24 completed cycles the error was 4 to 7%, within the stated caveat, but f* 0.50 stopped after one completed cycle plus 0.86 of the next, so per-completed-cycle figures were 1.86 times too high. event_time is the next pending event's time within the cycle (the engine rebases time to zero at each cycle end), so it slightly overstates the time reached; the field-recorder frame count (32 frames per cycle) gives 1.84 covered cycles against 1.86, agreeing within about 1%.

decision: Stage 4 of the resting-contact method (line L0009): a moving stack's path is integrated in Python in spans and stored as per-sphere quartic pieces the compiled event loop reads; other spheres find their first contact with a stack sphere by conservative advancement on those pieces. A touch on a stack sphere slower than the rest speed joins the stack (the toucher's approach removed as a restitution-zero touch, booked as in D0085: half m vn^2 as pair loss, the rest as plate work and plate impulse); a faster touch, or a touch between two stacks, breaks the stack(s) (each sphere riding if it has a plate contact and the plate pushes, else free) and the ordinary collision happens at once. A contact opening splits the stack into parts still on the plate (stacks, or riders when one sphere is left) and free spheres. A span is cut where a stack sphere would leave its cell (sampled every 2e-4 diameters of motion; cells are at least 5e-4 wider than any sphere) or reach a side wall; at a wall the stack breaks.
alternatives: Leave the hit to the event queue after a break (tried first: a slow touch at the same instant rebuilt the stack first and the two alternated without time advancing)
Bounce faster hits off the stack sphere as if immovable (the design's rule for still spheres, D0074), keeping the stack
Join every touch regardless of speed
rationale: Mirrors the design's rule for a hit riding sphere (design.md section 6, item 2): below the rest speed a capture into the stack, above it the rider becomes free and the ordinary collision happens. Stack spheres are moving riders, so the same rule applies. Breaking and colliding at once is needed so time advances.

decision: Stack spans are integrated lazily: the first span of a stack covers 0.01 time units, each span that ends uninterrupted doubles the next, and the integrator's last step size carries over between spans.
alternatives: Integrate each span to the run's stop time (tried first: in the stall layer each stack was integrated to the cycle's end and then interrupted within about 0.001 time units, so nearly all of the Python work was thrown away)
rationale: A cost setting: the stack's motion is the same differential equation solved at round-off tolerance either way; only where the integrator restarts changes, at the 1e-12 level. Nothing physical depends on 0.01.

decision: When a sphere joins a moving stack by a slow touch, the touch is a restitution-zero impulse over the whole new stack: the smallest mass-weighted change of all its spheres' velocities, by normal impulses only at its contacts, the plate immovable, that leaves no contact closing (contacts that would pull are dropped, an active-set solve). The plate's impulse and work are booked; the rest of the energy change is booked as pair loss (never a gain in the plate frame). This replaces D0087's rule of changing only the joining sphere.
alternatives: Change only the joining sphere (D0087). In E0104 seed 1 this gave a joining riding sphere a vertical velocity off the plate's (about 9e-4), so it sank 3.17e-6 into the plate over the stack's life; handing it back put it on the plate and into the sphere above it by 1.53e-6, the overlap error.
Change only the touched stack sphere: wrong when it is itself held by the plate or by others.
rationale: The plate holds riders, so a touch on a riding sphere has to be taken up by the spheres the plate does not hold; solving all contacts together does this, and it also answers the checker's point that D0087 treated the stack as immovable at a touch.

decision: Per-cycle event cost of an E0089 step is taken from each completed cycle's own count in audit.json, quoted as cheap-cycle and expensive-cycle means and as the mean per pair of cycles (one of each, complete pairs from the step's first cycle). For a step stopped on the CPU cap the unfinished cycle is given separately, as a lower bound: step total from counters.json differences minus the completed cycles, with the fraction of a cycle it covered. Covered cycles (D0086) remain only as the divisor for counters kept per step (collisions, tiny collisions). Tool: tools/e0089_cycle_table.py; evidence/E0089-cycle-table.json.
alternatives: Keep dividing step totals by covered cycles (D0086): 18% too high at f* 0.33 and wrong in kind at f* 0.44 and 0.50, where one cheap cycle and one partial expensive cycle were averaged.
Per completed cycle: counts part of an unfinished cycle.
rationale: Under period doubling the cost of a step's unfinished cycle depends on whether it is a cheap or an expensive one, so no single per-cycle average of a stopped step is right; the checker showed this from audit.json (reviews/2026-11-25-L0015-2.json).
